problem: LLMs lack real-world grounding and their outputs are opaque and unpredictable, while prior language-grounded robot navigation (CoW, VLMaps, SayCan, PaLM-E) is not tested on contextual commands, often needs pre-built maps, and end-to-end models lack planning guarantees and explainability.
motivation: Search-and-rescue and human-robot teaming need high-bandwidth natural-language commands, including ones that require background knowledge (e.g. 'find something to help a firefighter'). Generating executable code as an intermediate layer between an LLM and classical planners gives interpretability and lets the LLM's priors be used with a real robot.
key_idea: Extend ViperGPT-style code generation to embodied navigation: GPT-3.5 writes Python against an API of object detection (GLIP) and a navigation client, whose output 2D object coordinates are projected onto an online lidar 3D map and passed to a graph-based planner.
insight: A concatenated semi-panoramic image (A) beats separate left/front/right frames (B) at 90% vs 66% code-and-detection success on 50 classroom sentences, because separate frames break cross-frame spatial ordering (e.g. sorting 'middle outlet' over merged, overlapping coordinates). Failures in the real-world tests concentrate in object detection and waypoint projection rather than code generation or planning (100% of planned paths were followed), and the harder command classes (relational and contextual) fail most often. Literal interpretation of commands such as 'go to the second floor' shows the LLM lacks 3D spatial reasoning.
method: Command-to-code layer: GPT-3.5 receives a Python API prompt (ImagePatch with find/exists/verify_property/simple_query/compute_depth, plus a navigate_to_object nav client) adapted from ViperGPT, and generates code returning a dict with function, pixel-center inputs and bounding box.
Visual grounding: GLIP object detector executed inside the generated code on the RGB input to resolve which object the command refers to; detector is substitutable.
Input representation: compares (A) three cameras (left/front/right) stitched into one padded image with the order stated in the prompt vs (B) separate frames processed individually.
3D projection: the object's image-center pixel is ray-cast onto an OctoMap 3D map built online with LIO-SAM lidar-inertial odometry, giving a 3D waypoint.

Graph-based planner: sample-and-project planner (from Ahmad et al. / Biggie et al.) samples a graph by robot dimensions, selects the best path to the waypoint, and replans to the graph boundary if no path exists.
Command taxonomy: sentences categorized as Generic, Specific, Relational, Contextual for evaluation, with per-stage success (Code, OD, WP, Path&Exec).

setting.backbone: GPT-3.5 (frozen) for code generation + GLIP object detector (frozen)
setting.observation: 3 RGB cameras giving semi-panoramic view + 64-beam Ouster lidar + IMU, with an online 3D map
setting.action_space: 3D waypoint output by the intermediate layer, converted by a graph-based planner into a continuous trajectory

numbers.eval_set_note: 114 sentences across Theater, Lobby, Outdoor, Courtyard
numbers.extra: real Boston Dynamics Spot; some extra objects placed in scenes
success = correct code and correct object on map

numbers_note: Custom real-robot evaluation; no standard benchmark. Per-category and per-scene breakdowns are in Tables 2/3 (e.g. Contextual Path&Exec 41.38, Generic 68.18; Outdoor 70.83, Lobby 44.83).
results: On 114 real-world commands across four environments, NavCon reaches 78.07% code generation, 63.16% object detection, 58.77% waypoint projection and 57.89% path and execution success. Concatenated images give 90% vs 66% for separate frames in a classroom test. No standard baselines were compared.
limitations: Reasoning is only in 2D image space, so relations such as 'behind' or 'right of' are weak, and the LLM misreads 3D concepts (e.g. 'second floor').
Object detection and 3D projection errors (long range 10-12 m, lidar-camera calibration) dominate failures, and contextual/relational commands perform worst (41% and 57% path success).
No baseline comparison and a small, hand-written test set; single-goal commands only, no sequential instructions or exploration.
builds_on: Graph-based planner (Ahmad et al. / Biggie et al.)
